valuation.quote_listing: NASDAQ (FIP, the U.S. listing and only listing)

bull_thesis: FTAI Infrastructure is a collection of hard, cash-generating assets — freight railroads, two export terminals, and (for now) a power plant — that the market is valuing well below the sum of its parts. The bull case is a two-part re-rating driven by a management team that has, so far, done exactly what it said it would. First, the de-risking event is real and dated: in late April the company signed a binding agreement to sell its Long Ridge power business to Mara Holdings for $1.52 billion, with more than $300 million of net cash flowing to the parent after the plant's own debt is repaid or assumed, and management says there are no material conditions to closing beyond routine regulatory sign-off, with the deal expected to close in the third quarter of 2026. That cash is earmarked to pay down the most expensive debt — the roughly $1.35 billion parent term loan that carries a 9.75% coupon — cutting parent interest expense by about $30 million a year and lifting free cash flow. Second, what remains is a cleaner, faster-growing freight-rail company. The 2025 acquisition of the Wheeling & Lake Erie Railway has consistently beaten plan (fourth-quarter 2025 rail EBITDA of $41.3 million, with the Wheeling's own EBITDA up 34% year over year), management is targeting a combined Transtar-plus-Wheeling run-rate of at least $220 million by the end of 2026, and the Nippon/U.S. Steel commitment of $11 billion of new steel investment (roughly $5 billion aimed at Transtar-served Mon Valley and Gary works) should add carloads over time. Freight railroads are franchise assets — captive shippers, irreplaceable track, high regulatory barriers — that have historically traded around 15 times EBITDA, and management is buying bolt-ons (the $45 million Tidewater Logistics deal closed June 29, 2026, plus four more rail targets under evaluation) at far lower multiples. On top of the rail engine sit two export terminals with their own growth: Jefferson is running near a $60 million annual EBITDA rate with a path management describes to over $100 million from three new pieces of business, and Repauno's Phase 2 project is contracted for roughly $80 million of annual EBITDA once it starts up in early 2027, with a permitted Phase 3 expansion behind it. Management has flagged both terminals as future monetization candidates in 2026-2027. Full-year adjusted EBITDA has roughly doubled, from $127.6 million in 2024 to $232.3 million in 2025, with an exit run-rate above $320 million. If the rail business re-rates toward peer multiples as the terminals ramp and the balance sheet delevers, a sum-of-the-parts value in the $8-plus range is achievable. The key conditions: the Long Ridge sale closes on terms and on time, the rail integration keeps beating plan, and the terminals hit their contracted ramps without construction slippage.
bear_thesis: The bear case is that FIP common stock is a thin, highly-leveraged slice of equity sitting on top of a mountain of debt, and that the sum-of-the-parts math only works if you assume a rich rail multiple that the market plainly does not grant. Start with the balance sheet: net debt was about $3.68 billion at March 31, 2026 (total debt $3.91 billion against just $227 million of cash), and even after the Long Ridge sale pays down roughly $300 million, the parent still carries a ~$1.05 billion term loan at 9.75%, on top of a separate $1 billion of preferred stock held by Ares at the rail subsidiary (a 10% dividend, ahead of common). Cash generation does not yet cover the build-out: trailing-twelve-month free cash flow was negative $363 million and trailing diluted earnings per share were negative $4.47, because the terminals are still swallowing capital. That leverage is what makes the equity a stub — value the rail business at a conservative 10-to-11 times its targeted EBITDA and almost all of it is absorbed by the $1 billion rail preferred and the parent term loan, leaving little for common holders, and the two terminals carry so much of their own debt (Jefferson alone has had roughly $0.8-1.0 billion against $60 million of EBITDA) that their equity value is near zero until earnings actually ramp. The market has already seen the Long Ridge announcement and the stock did not re-rate — it sits near its 52-week low of $3.90, down more than 40% from its high, which tells you investors treat the sale proceeds as debt service, not equity creation. There is also a governance tell: on the open market, insiders sold far more than they bought (one seller of about 3.4 million shares against four buyers of 540,000 shares). The dividend is a token $0.03 a quarter. And much of the bull case rests on forward run-rates and 'line of sight' targets rather than delivered numbers, so any construction delay at Repauno, softer steel volumes at Transtar, a lower-than-hoped rail multiple, or slippage in the Long Ridge close would leave a company that is still burning cash with a stub equity that can fall well below today's price. What would confirm the bear: the Long Ridge deal slips or re-prices, rail EBITDA stalls short of the $220 million target, or the terminals miss their contracted start dates while the 9.75% parent debt keeps compounding.
sop_breakdown: Built as a sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately, then netting parent debt), on roughly 118 million shares. RAIL (Transtar + Wheeling + Tidewater): base ~$200M forward EBITDA at ~12.5x = ~$2.5B enterprise value, minus the $1.0B Ares preferred at the rail entity = ~$1.5B of equity to FIP; this is the dominant value driver and the single biggest swing factor (10x vs 15x moves the whole answer). LONG RIDGE: signed sale to Mara for $1.52B aggregate; after the plant's own debt is repaid/assumed, >$300M of net cash to the parent — modeled as a debt paydown rather than retained cash to avoid double-counting. JEFFERSON: ~$60-100M EBITDA at ~9x = ~$0.5-0.9B enterprise value, but ~$0.8B of segment debt leaves thin equity (~$75M base, ~$0 in a bad case). REPAUNO: Phase 2 contracted ~$80M EBITDA (not yet operational) at ~8x, less ~$0.37B debt and a timing haircut = ~$150M base equity; Phase 3 is unpriced optionality. PARENT: ~$1.05B term loan (post-Long-Ridge paydown) at 9.75% is a drag, partly offset by modest holdco cash. Netting: rail equity ~$1.5B + Jefferson ~$0.08B + Repauno ~$0.15B + holdco cash ~$0.05B minus ~$1.05B parent debt ≈ $0.73B of common equity, or ~$6 per share. The bear (~$2.75) applies an ~11x rail multiple and floors terminal equity near zero; the bull (~$8.50) applies ~14-15x rail, full terminal ramps, and Phase 3 optionality.
risk_reward: Skewed favorably on the analytical sum-of-the-parts, but the equity is a levered stub, so both tails are wide. At ~$4.50 the stock trades roughly a third below a ~$6 base-case sum-of-the-parts, and the near-term catalyst — closing the signed $1.52 billion Long Ridge sale in the third quarter of 2026 — is a genuine, dated de-risking event that pays down the 9.75% parent debt. The upside toward $8-plus requires the rail business to re-rate toward the mid-teens multiple management argues for while the terminals ramp on contracted volumes. The downside toward the high-$2s is not a going-concern story but a de-rating one: because roughly $1 billion of rail preferred and ~$1 billion of parent debt sit ahead of common, a lower rail multiple plus disappointing terminal equity leaves little for shareholders. Management's delivery record on its 2025 objectives is the main reason to weight the base and bull cases more heavily, but the persistent discount, negative free cash flow, and net open-market insider selling are the reasons not to underwrite the bull case in full.
peer_comps_note: The provided peer file lists genuine business comparables — GATX and Trinity (rail), Brookfield Infrastructure (multi-asset infra holding company), and energy-logistics cash-flow names such as USA Compression, Cheniere Partners, Atlantica, and NextEra Energy Partners — but flags FIP as 'unmapped' because the radar dataset carries no populated valuation, growth, or margin fields for it, so a quantified relative-cheapness rank cannot be computed from that source. Qualitatively the peer note is right that FTAI-family spinoffs run elevated leverage and capex-heavy build-outs that depress near-term free-cash-flow multiples versus mature toll-road-style infrastructure — a real feature of this story, not obviously a mispricing. The load-bearing external anchor here is management's own multiple argument: freight railroads have historically traded around 15 times EBITDA, and FIP is acquiring bolt-on rail at high single-digit to low double-digit multiples. My base case deliberately uses a below-peer ~12.5x on the rail segment to stay disciplined given the leverage and forward-run-rate nature of the EBITDA.
forcing_function: The specific event to wait for is the close of the Long Ridge sale to Mara Holdings — a signed, binding $1.52 billion agreement with more than $300 million of net proceeds to the parent, management-guided to close in the third quarter of 2026 with no material conditions beyond regulatory approval. As of July 10, 2026 it has not yet closed (Long Ridge still reported its own first-quarter 2026 results as a FIP portfolio company on June 11). The close is the hard, dated event that converts the sum-of-the-parts thesis into cash: it pays down the 9.75% parent term loan by ~$300 million, cuts interest expense by ~$30 million a year, and proves out the deleveraging path. Secondary forcing functions that would extend the re-rating: a rail acquisition or a Jefferson/Repauno monetization announcement (management has teed both up for 2026-2027), and the end-2026 rail EBITDA run-rate print approaching the $220 million target.
moderator_conclusion: This is a real sum-of-the-parts discount attached to a management team that has earned credibility by delivering on a demanding 2025 to-do list — consolidating Long Ridge, acquiring and integrating the Wheeling ahead of plan, refinancing the holdco, funding Repauno Phase 2, and now signing the Long Ridge sale it promised for the first half of 2026. The base-case sum-of-the-parts is about $6 a share against a ~$4.50 price, and the near-term catalyst is a genuine hard, dated event: the $1.52 billion Long Ridge sale is expected to close in the third quarter of 2026 and delivers over $300 million of deleveraging. Where I stop short of an aggressive buy is the capital structure. FIP common is a thin, highly-leveraged stub: net debt of about $3.68 billion, roughly $1 billion of rail preferred ahead of common, a ~$1.05 billion post-close parent loan at 9.75%, trailing free cash flow of negative $363 million, and negative trailing earnings per share. The whole sum-of-the-parts answer swings on the rail multiple, and the market — which already saw the Long Ridge announcement and left the stock near its 52-week low — is plainly not granting the mid-teens multiple the bull case needs. Net open-market insider selling reinforces caution. My call is to wait for the wash-out to clear: the thesis is real, but I want the confirming event — the Long Ridge close and the parent-debt paydown landing in the third quarter of 2026 — before sizing up, rather than underwriting forward run-rates through a levered stub. The value case, judged on its own without the catalyst overlay, is a moderate one: a genuine discount to a parts-based value, but capped by heavy leverage and negative free cash flow, so a middling value conviction is honest. The rail assets carry a narrow but durable franchise moat (captive industrial shippers, irreplaceable track, regulatory barriers), the terminals add location advantages, and no structural secular force threatens the terminal value in a terminal way — the power exposure is being sold and the remaining businesses skew toward freight rail and growing natural-gas-liquid and ammonia exports.
